# 2 Maccabees Chapter 4 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_004_page_001.jpg

---

**1** The Simon mentioned above, who had denounced the funds and his own country, slandered Onias as if it were he who had incited Heliodorus and who was behind the whole trouble.

**2** He had the audacity to call this man — this benefactor of the city, protector of his fellow countrymen, and zealot for the laws — an enemy of the state.

**3** But when his hostility went so far that murders were being carried out by some of Simon's associates,

**4** Onias recognized the danger of the rivalry, and that Apollonius, son of Menestheus and governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was intensifying Simon's malice.

**5** So Onias betook himself to the king — not to be an accuser of his fellow citizens, but with a view to the common welfare and well-being of all the people.

**6** For he saw that without the king's attention, it would be impossible to achieve stability in public affairs or to put a stop to Simon's madness.

**7** But when Seleucus died and Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, succeeded to the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias obtained the high priesthood through corrupt means,

**8** promising the king three hundred and sixty talents of silver and eighty talents from some other source of revenue.

**9** Beyond this he promised to pay a hundred and fifty more if authority were given him to establish a gymnasium and a corps of young men and to register the people of Jerusalem as Antiochene citizens.

**10** When the king gave his consent and Jason came to power, he immediately shifted his compatriots to the Greek way of life.

**11** Setting aside the royal privileges that had been secured for the Jews through John, father of Eupolemus — who had gone on the mission to establish friendship and alliance with the Romans — he abolished the lawful forms of life and introduced customs contrary to the law.

**12** With obvious delight he established a gymnasium right under the citadel itself, and led the noblest of the young men to wear the broad-brimmed Greek hat.

**13** There was such an extreme of Hellenization and adoption of foreign customs, thanks to the surpassing wickedness of Jason, who was godless and no true high priest,

**14** that the priests were no longer zealous for the service of the altar. Despising the sanctuary and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the unlawful activities in the wrestling arena when the call of the discus sounded,

**15** thinking nothing of what their ancestors had held in honor and regarding the Greek forms of prestige as the finest thing of all.

**16** For this very reason a heavy disaster came upon them, and the men whose conduct and manner of life they had so earnestly emulated and desired to imitate became their enemies and punished them.

**17** For it is no light thing to be impious toward the divine laws — and the time that follows will make this plain.

**18** When the quinquennial games were being held at Tyre and the king was present,

**19** the vile Jason sent delegates as spectators, bearing three hundred drachmas of silver for the sacrifice to Hercules. But even the bearers thought it improper to use the money for a sacrifice, considering it unsuitable for that purpose.

**20** So the sum intended by the sender for the sacrifice to Hercules was, by the decision of the bearers, redirected to the construction of triremes.

**21** When Apollonius son of Menestheus was sent to Egypt for the coronation of Philometor as king, Antiochus, learning that Philometor had become hostile to his government, took thought for his own security. He went to Joppa and then traveled on to Jerusalem.

**22** He was received with great ceremony by Jason and the city, being welcomed with torchlight and acclamations, and afterward he led his army into Phoenicia.

**23** After an interval of three years, Jason sent Menelaus — the brother of the Simon mentioned above — to bring the money to the king and to obtain decisions on certain pressing matters.

**24** But once Menelaus gained an audience with the king and saw his opportunity in appearing as a man of considerable dignity, he diverted the high priesthood to himself, outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver.

**25** He came back with the royal commission, but with nothing worthy of the high priesthood. He had the disposition of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.

**26** So Jason, who had ousted his own brother, was himself ousted by another man and driven as a fugitive into the territory of the Ammonites.

**27** Menelaus held the office but paid nothing of what he had promised to the king,

**28** in spite of demands from Sostratus, the commander of the citadel, who was responsible for collecting the revenues. For this reason both men were summoned before the king.

**29** Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as his deputy in the high priesthood, while Sostratus left Crates, the commander of the Cyprian troops.

**30** Meanwhile, it happened that the people of Tarsus and of Mallus revolted because their cities had been given as a present to Antiochis, the king's concubine.

**31** So the king went in haste to settle the matter, leaving Andronicus, a man of high rank, as his viceroy.

**32** Menelaus, thinking he had found a good opportunity, presented to Andronicus some gold vessels from the temple — some of which he had already sold to Tyre and to the surrounding cities.

**33** When Onias learned of this, he brought the charge openly, having first withdrawn for safety to the sanctuary of Daphne near Antioch.

**34** So Menelaus took Andronicus aside and pressed him to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias and, extending false assurances and pledging with an oath while giving his right hand, persuaded him — despite his suspicions — to leave the sanctuary. He immediately put him to death, with no regard for justice.

**35** At this, not only the Jews but many from other nations as well were outraged and deeply aggrieved at the unjust killing of this man.

**36** When the king returned from the region of Cilicia, the Jews in the city — together with Greeks who shared their indignation — appealed to him, grieved that Onias had been murdered without any cause.

**37** Antiochus was genuinely grieved and moved to compassion; he wept because of the sober and restrained character of the deceased.

**38** Inflamed with anger, he stripped Andronicus of his purple robe immediately, tore off his outer garments, and led him through the whole city to the very spot where he had committed the outrage against Onias. There he executed the murderer. The LORD repaid him with the punishment he deserved.

**39** When many acts of sacrilege had been committed throughout the city by Lysimachus with the approval of Menelaus, and when news of these spread abroad, the people assembled against Lysimachus — since large numbers of gold vessels had already been dispersed.

**40** When the crowds rose in revolt and were filled with anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and launched a violent unjust attack, with a certain Auranus as leader — a man as advanced in age as he was advanced in foolishness.

**41** When those under attack realized what was happening, some grabbed stones, some seized pieces of wood, some scooped up handfuls of the ashes that lay nearby, and they hurled everything at Lysimachus and his men in wild confusion.

**42** As a result, they wounded many and killed some, and they put all the rest to flight. The temple robber himself they killed beside the treasury.

**43** Charges were brought against Menelaus in connection with the whole affair.

**44** When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the council of elders laid the case before him.

**45** But Menelaus, already virtually convicted, promised a large sum of money to Ptolemy son of Dorymenes to win over the king.

**46** Ptolemy, taking the king aside into a colonnade as if for refreshment, induced him to change his position.

**47** Menelaus — the very source of all the trouble — he acquitted of all the charges; while those unfortunate men, who would have been released without penalty had they pleaded before Scythians, he condemned to death.

**48** So those who had spoken up for the city and the villages and the sacred vessels quickly met with unjust punishment.

**49** Even the Tyrians were so outraged at the crime that they provided generously for the men's burial.

**50** As for Menelaus, he remained in office through the greed of those in power, growing ever more wicked, proving to be the chief schemer against his own fellow citizens.
